Numerical validation, conventions and scope

Source: vignettes/numerical-validation.Rmd
numerical-validation.Rmd
library(controlcompR)

A control package is only useful if its numbers can be trusted. This article states the conventions, explains how results are verified, lists what is implemented, experimental, planned or unsupported, and describes the limits of every guarantee.

Conventions

quantity convention
continuous Lyapunov A X + X A^\top + Q = 0 (same as python-control and MATLAB lyap)
discrete Lyapunov A X A^\top - X + Q = 0
CARE A^\top P + P A - (PB + N) R^{-1} (B^\top P + N^\top) + Q = 0, stabilizing solution
DARE A^\top P A - P - (A^\top P B + N)(R + B^\top P B)^{-1}(B^\top P A + N^\top) + Q = 0
LQR law u = -Kx
Kalman P prior covariance P_{k|k-1}; Z is the posterior P_{k|k}
Kalman M, L measurement update gain and one-step predictor gain
feedback ctrl_feedback(G, K) is (I + GK)^{-1}G, negative by default
series ctrl_series(G1, G2) is G_2 G_1 (signal flows from 1 to 2)
margins loop gain L under unity negative feedback
frequency units rad/s (rad/sample divided by dt for discrete models)
discrete time dt > 0 is the sample interval; dt = 0 is continuous
MPC decision vector (x_0, \ldots, x_N, u_0, \ldots, u_{N-1}), u_k acts between x_k and x_{k+1}
H-infinity norm peak of the largest singular value over frequency; Inf for unstable models
H2 norm Inf for unstable models or continuous models with direct feedthrough

Algorithms

Numerically sensitive computations use orthogonal decompositions and avoid explicitly forming squared or ill-conditioned quantities. Many results are checked after the fact, but the checks detect failures; they do not prove backward stability for every input. The main methods:

  • Riccati equations: ordered real Schur decomposition of the Hamiltonian (continuous) or symplectic pencil (discrete, generalized Schur), with the stabilizing subspace selected by eigenvalue location. The relative residual (accepted up to 1e-6) and the closed-loop eigenvalues are verified; a solution that fails either check raises an error instead of being returned.
  • Lyapunov and Stein equations: real Schur form, then Bartels-Stewart (continuous) or block back substitution (discrete).
  • Controllability and observability: orthogonal staircase forms (never the rank of the controllability matrix, which is numerically meaningless beyond small systems).
  • Gramians and Hankel singular values: Cholesky factors of the Gramians computed directly by Hammarling’s method on the complex Schur form, so the Gramians are never formed and their condition number is never squared; the H2 norm is \|C L_c\|_F with the same factor.
  • H-infinity norm: the Bruinsma-Steinbuch level-set iteration on the Hamiltonian, with the imaginary-axis eigenvalue test.
  • Discretization: matrix exponential of an augmented matrix (zero-order and first-order hold), bilinear (Tustin) and matched pole-zero transformations.
  • Frequency response: a complex linear solve per frequency on a diagonally balanced state-space model. Transfer function objects are evaluated from their polynomial coefficients, which is accurate for low orders; convert high-order transfer functions to state space first (ctrl_tf2ss()) for better conditioning.
  • Pole placement: robust eigenstructure assignment (Kautsky, Nichols and Van Dooren), with the eigenvalues of the result verified.
  • QPs: OSQP with tight tolerances and solution polishing; every MPC step reports the solver status, bound violation and dynamics residual.
A <- matrix(c(0, 1, -2, -3), 2, byrow = TRUE)
B <- matrix(c(0, 1))
sol <- ctrl_care(A, B, diag(2), 1)
sol$residual
#> [1] 1.720524e-15
sol$poles
#> [1] -1.000000+0i -2.236068+0i

Tolerances

Rank decisions and structural tests use relative tolerances based on the size and the norm of the problem, of the form \mathrm{tol} = c\, n^2\, \varepsilon\, \|M\| for the staircase forms. Stability is decided on a state realization balanced together with its input and output matrices, with per-pole bands from the first-order eigenvalue error bound, so the decision does not depend on state units. Covariance matrices are inverted on their support after equilibration (scaling to unit diagonal), so a small but positive variance is never treated as zero. Boundary cases are reported ("marginally stable" for linear models, "inconclusive" for equilibria of nonlinear models) instead of being forced into stable or unstable. Every function that takes a tolerance documents it.

Testing strategy

The test suite checks results against properties that must hold, rather than against stored numbers:

  • residuals of matrix equations and the eigenvalues of closed loops;
  • invariance under similarity transformations (poles, zeros, Hankel singular values, norms);
  • identities: series and feedback algebra, the separation principle for LQG, ctrl_ss2tf(ctrl_tf2ss(G)) equals G;
  • exact cross-checks between independent algorithms: MPC without active constraints equals LQR with the Riccati terminal weight, MHE without active constraints equals the Kalman filter, the H2 norm from the Gramian factor equals the integral of the frequency response, the H-infinity norm equals the peak of a dense frequency sweep;
  • analytic results: first and second order step responses, Ziegler-Nichols tables, balanced truncation error bounds;
  • invariance under changes of units: diagonal and orthogonal state scalings, input and cost scalings and time scalings leave Riccati solutions, Hankel singular values, norms, stability decisions, Kalman, UKF, smoother and MHE posteriors unchanged (including covariances whose entries span many orders of magnitude);
  • rejection of invalid problems: indefinite weights, unstabilizable pairs, singular measurement noise, ill-posed interconnections, infeasible QPs, nonfinite inputs and arithmetic that overflows.
G <- ctrl_ss(matrix(c(-1, 2, 0, -3), 2), matrix(c(1, 0)), matrix(c(0, 1), 1))
T <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 1), 2)
G2 <- ctrl_ss(T %*% G$A %*% solve(T), T %*% G$B, G$C %*% solve(T))
c(ctrl_norm(G, "inf"), ctrl_norm(G2, "inf"))
#> [1] 0.6666667 0.6666667
rbind(ctrl_hsvd(G), ctrl_hsvd(G2))
#>           [,1]       [,2]
#> [1,] 0.3871459 0.05381261
#> [2,] 0.3871459 0.05381261

Reference comparison

The repository contains benchmarks/reference/: a set of problems (problems.json), a Python script that solves them with python-control and slycot (the SLICOT Fortran library), and an R script that compares controlcompR’s results. The comparison runs on GitHub Actions; it covers continuous and discrete Riccati and Lyapunov equations, H-infinity and H2 norms, Hankel singular values, zero-order hold discretization, pole placement and H-infinity synthesis. Relative errors are required to be below 10^{-7} (and 10^{-3} for the bisection level of H-infinity synthesis, where both packages stop at a tolerance).

area status notes

poles, zeros, controllability, observability, minimal realization implemented staircase forms
Lyapunov and Riccati equations implemented residual and stability checks
time responses (step, impulse, initial, arbitrary input) implemented exact zero-order hold for sampled inputs
frequency responses, margins, disk margins, norms implemented
LQR (continuous, discrete, finite horizon) implemented
pole placement and observers implemented
Kalman filter, smoother, LQG implemented
PID with filter, anti-windup, bumpless transfer, tuning rules implemented
linear MPC (bounds, rates, soft constraints, terminal sets) implemented OSQP
offset-free MPC and MHE implemented
balanced truncation and residualization implemented stable part; unstable part kept
ARX, subspace identification, validation tools implemented other model structures through sysid
H2 synthesis implemented continuous time, D_{11} = 0
H-infinity synthesis experimental continuous time, D_{11} = 0, every result checked against the upper bound of an independent norm computation
nonlinear simulation, linearization, equilibria implemented
EKF and UKF implemented
nonlinear MPC experimental single shooting, local optimum
discrete time H-infinity synthesis planned refused with an error
general D_{11} in H-infinity synthesis planned refused with an error

explicit MPC, robust tube MPC unsupported
descriptor (E \ne I) systems unsupported
hybrid and switched systems unsupported

What the guarantees cover

A guarantee in this package is a mathematical statement about a model. LQR optimality, MPC constraint satisfaction, H-infinity bounds and robust stability tests all hold for the model and the uncertainty description that were given. None of them covers unmodeled dynamics, sensor faults, timing jitter, quantization or a wrong model. Verify every design in simulation with realistic disturbances and noise, and treat deployment to a physical system as an engineering task with its own safety analysis. This package does not generate certified code for embedded targets.
